hooks.text: We shortened an asteroid's orbit thirty-two minutes just by crashing into it.
Can a deliberate spacecraft crash actually nudge a moonlet off course?
NASA just pushed a giant space rock seven million miles from Earth.

title: How We Steered an Asteroid
description: NASA's DART mission successfully changed the orbit of the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos by crashing a spacecraft into it at 14,000 miles per hour.

beats.text: We shortened an asteroid's orbit thirty-two minutes just by crashing into it.
beats.visual: artist's concept of the DART spacecraft impact on Dimorphos, 2022

beats.text: In September 2022, NASA slammed a box-shaped spacecraft into Dimorphos, a moonlet seven million miles from Earth.
beats.visual: diagram of the Didymos and Dimorphos asteroid system, 2022

beats.text: The DART mission targeted this 530-foot-wide rock at a staggering speed of 14,000 miles per hour.
beats.visual: DRACO camera final pre-impact image of Dimorphos surface, 2022

beats.text: While telescopes like James Webb watched, an Italian CubeSat caught the moment the probe hit the surface.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope view of the DART impact ejecta plume, 2022

beats.text: Mission controllers only expected the violent collision to nudge the asteroid orbit by about seventy-three seconds.
beats.visual: James Webb Space Telescope view of the DART impact plume, 2022
queries: James Webb Space Telescope NIRCam DART

beats.text: But the impact blasted so much debris into space that the recoil acted like a massive rocket engine.
beats.visual: LICIACube snapshot of the asteroid ejecta plume, 2022
queries: Light Italian CubeSat for Imaging of Asteroids image

beats.text: This amplified the push so much that the nearly twelve-hour orbit changed by over half an hour.
beats.visual: diagram showing the orbital change of Dimorphos after DART impact, 2022

beats.text: This is how we learned to steer a giant space rock by crashing into it.
beats.visual: ESA Hera mission artist's concept arriving at Didymos, 2026
